title: Sandwich loaf
skill: Kneading to a windowpane, baking a loaf

notes.2: Makes 2 loaves. Knead the dough in two halves, and you'll need two loaf pans.

move.title: Kneaded to a windowpane
move.body: A soft sandwich loaf needs strong gluten to rise tall in its pan. Today you'll knead until a piece of dough stretches thin enough to see light through, shape it into a tight log, and bake it until the center reads 190°F.

callback.body: Pita's dough rises once, then bakes flat and fast. A loaf rises twice, the second time in its pan, and bakes for half an hour, so it needs more kneading to hold its shape that long.

why.title: Milk and butter
why.body: Milk and butter make an enriched dough. Their fat coats the gluten strands, so the crumb is soft and fine instead of chewy, and milk sugar helps the crust brown.

why.title: The windowpane test
why.body: Stretch a small piece of dough slowly between your fingers. When the gluten is fully developed, it goes thin enough to let light through without tearing. That's the strength a tall loaf needs.

why.title: Roll it tight
why.body: Rolling the dough up tightly stretches its surface, like a balloon skin. A tight skin holds the gas in and pushes the loaf up into a dome. A loose roll leaves gaps that bake into holes.

why.title: An inch above the rim
why.body: The loaf rises a little more in the oven, then sets. Baked when it's about an inch above the pan's rim, it ends tall but doesn't overflow or collapse.

why.title: 190°F inside
why.body: At 190°F, the starch in the center has set. Below that, the middle bakes up wet and dense. A deep brown top doesn't prove it's done; the thermometer does.

why.title: Cool before slicing
why.body: A hot loaf is still finishing inside. Steam is moving out through the crumb. Slice it now and the steam escapes all at once, leaving the middle gummy.

wrong.sign: The dough tears instead of stretching thin
wrong.fix: Keep kneading, 2 minutes at a time, and test again.

wrong.sign: The loaf is short and dense
wrong.fix: The dough didn't rise enough before baking, or the gluten wasn't developed. Next time, wait until it's an inch above the rim, and knead to a full windowpane.

wrong.sign: The top split along one side
wrong.fix: It went into the oven a little early. Next time give it 10 more minutes on the second rise.

wrong.sign: The top is brown, but the center reads under 190°F
wrong.fix: Lay foil loosely over the top and bake 5 more minutes.

wrong.sign: A big hole runs under the top crust
wrong.fix: The log was rolled loosely. Roll the next one tighter and pinch the seam well.

quiz.q: What tells you the dough is kneaded enough?
choices: A piece stretches thin enough to see light through
quiz.explain: That's the windowpane test. The gluten is strong enough to hold a tall rise.

quiz.q: When does the loaf go in the oven?
choices: When it's about an inch above the pan's rim
quiz.explain: It rises a little more in the oven, then sets.

quiz.q: Why let the loaf cool before slicing?
choices: It's still finishing inside, and slicing hot makes it gummy
quiz.explain: Steam is still moving out through the crumb.

ingredients.text: a little more, for the bowl and pan

steps.text: Warm the milk in the measuring cup in the microwave for about 40 seconds. Stir it and check it with the thermometer. It should read 105 to 110°F.
steps.tip: Too hot? Let it sit a minute and check again.

steps.text: Pour the milk into the large bowl. Stir in the sugar, then sprinkle the yeast over the top. Leave it alone to bloom.
steps.look: Foam on top, and it smells like bread.

steps.text: Add the softened butter, the salt, and the flour. Stir with the wooden spoon until a shaggy dough forms.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. Raw flour can make you sick.

steps.text: Dust the counter with flour and turn the dough out. Knead it until it's smooth and stretchy, then do the windowpane test. If it tears, knead 2 more minutes and test again.
steps.look: A small piece stretches thin enough to see light through without tearing.

steps.text: Butter the bowl, put the dough in, and turn it once to coat it. Cover with a towel and leave it somewhere warm until it doubles.
steps.look: Doubled. A floured finger pressed in leaves a dent that stays.

steps.text: Butter the loaf pan. Press the dough out on the counter and roll it into a rectangle about 8 by 10 inches. Starting from a short side, roll it up tightly into a log, pressing as you go. Pinch the seam closed and set the log in the pan, seam down.
steps.tip: Press each turn of the roll down with your thumbs to seal it as you go.

steps.text: Cover the pan loosely with the towel and let the loaf proof. Heat the oven to 350°F while it does.
steps.look: The top has risen about 1 inch above the rim of the pan.

steps.text: Bake the loaf. Check it at 25 minutes, and if the top is already deep brown, lay a sheet of foil loosely over it.
With oven mitts, pull the pan out partway. Push the thermometer into the end of the loaf so the tip reaches the center. It's done at 190°F. If it's lower, bake 5 more minutes and check again.
Turn off the oven. Let the loaf sit in the pan for 5 minutes, then tip it out onto the cooling rack with oven mitts on.
Let the loaf cool on the rack before you slice it. Slice it with the knife on the cutting board, using a gentle sawing motion.
